# Action and Control

::: {.callout-question}

How do decisions become safe, smooth motion?

:::

The robot reaches for the cup on the table by the child's hand. A jerky reach
overshoots and knocks it. A reach that starts a beat late arrives where the cup
was, not where it is. Neither failure is a number on a chart. One spills water on
a child, and the other is the difference between help and a hazard.

Action is where every property the book has traded becomes physical at the same
moment. The decision was made; now it has to move a body, in real time, without
crossing a line that must not be crossed. And here the book's sharpest claim comes
due: an AI choice is a control choice. The model you picked for speed back in the
perception chapter can decide whether this reach is safe.

## The dual brain, made physical

A control loop wants two things a learned model cannot promise: a fixed rate and
low jitter. A servo held to a smooth path needs its commands on a steady beat,
every few milliseconds, with little variation, or the motion judders and can go
unstable. A perception or deliberation model delivers answers on its own
schedule, tens to hundreds of milliseconds apart, and never exactly on time.

So you do not put the model in the control loop. The MCU runs the control loop at
a fixed rate and keeps the motion smooth, interpolating between targets. The MPU
decides what the target should be and hands it down when it is ready. Intent
flows from the cognitive side; the real-time side turns it into steady motion.
That is the boundary the board makes physical: hard real-time control on the MCU,
cognition on the MPU. It is worth being exact that this is not the same line as
the reflex-and-deliberation cascade of the earlier chapters. That cascade, the
fast model and the slow one, lives on the cognitive side, above the MCU; the
hardware split is real-time versus not, and the cascade rides on top of it.

::: {.column-margin}
**Properties in tension**: timeliness and safety, bounded by reliability. A wrong
move here is physical, not a label.
:::

## The safety envelope

Every motion keeps a margin between where it stops and where it would do harm.
That margin is not slack; it is a budget, and it has to cover every way the system
could be wrong. @fig-safety-envelope draws it. The margin must be at least the sum
of the errors that push the body past where it meant to stop:

$$\text{margin} \ge e_\text{sense} + e_\text{overshoot} + \underbrace{v\,t_\text{recover} + \frac{v^2}{2a}}_{\text{stopping distance}}$$

::: {#fig-safety-envelope fig-cap="**The safety envelope**: the margin from the commanded stop to the harm boundary must cover sensing error, overshoot, and the distance the body travels before a watchdog can stop it; quantizing the model grows the sensing error until the same margin no longer holds." fig-alt="A distance axis from a commanded stop to a harm boundary, with the gap labeled margin. Two stacked error bars start at the commanded stop, each made of sensing error, overshoot, and latency times speed. The 32-bit model's bar ends within the margin; the 8-bit model's bar has a much larger sensing-error segment and extends past the harm boundary."}
![](../assets/diagrams/safety-envelope.svg)
:::

Sensing error is how wrong the perception was about where things are. Overshoot
is how far the controller sails past its target, and it grows with timing jitter.
Sensing error and overshoot are the normal-operation terms: how wrong the
perception was about where things are, and how far a planned stop sails past its
target. The case that sizes the margin, though, is the failure. If the loop
hangs, the body keeps moving at speed $v$ not for one cycle but until the watchdog, the monitor that
trips a safe stop when the loop stops responding, catches it, the recovery time
$t_\text{recover}$ that a later chapter measures,
and only then covers the braking distance $v^2/2a$ as it decelerates at rate $a$.
That recovery time is far longer than a nominal cycle, and the braking term grows
with the square of the speed, which is why a slow watchdog and a fast body are
each dangerous, and why slowing the body down buys back margin faster than almost
anything else. Size the margin for that worst case, the conservative sum above,
and normal operation is covered for free.

## Why an AI choice is a control choice

Now the coupling. Look at the sensing-error term, and remember the knee from the
perception chapter. Quantizing the model from 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers was
how you bought latency and energy back. But quantization also lowers accuracy,
which means it raises $e_\text{sense}$. The second row of @fig-safety-envelope is
the same robot with the quantized model: the sensing-error segment grows, the
total error pushes past the harm boundary, and a margin that was safe at full
precision no longer is.

This is the claim that makes physical AI its own discipline rather than embedded
programming with a model attached. An optimization made for one property,
latency, silently spent another, safety, through a chain that crosses from
statistics into physics. The fix is not to refuse to quantize. It is to carry the
whole chain in one budget: if you shrink the model, you either widen the margin or
slow the body down, and you say which, with the number.

## Build

::: {.callout-build title="Make it smooth, then make it unsafe"}

Render one gesture two ways: a naive command straight to the target, and a smooth
interpolated trajectory between targets. Feel the difference, then measure it:
the jitter of the control loop and the overshoot of each version. Add a safe-stop
triggered by a bound, and measure the time to reach it.

Then close the loop on the chapter's claim. Take the perception model from the
knee lab and quantize it. Measure how much the sensing error grew, and feed that
into the margin inequality. Did the envelope still hold? If the body's speed is
fixed, how much wider does the margin have to be to absorb the new error?

A real safe-stop is unsafe to provoke on loaded hardware. Run it in simulation or
on an unloaded bench rig, plot the trajectory and the envelope, and treat the
crossing as the result whether or not a motor was turning.

:::

## What the number says

Smoothness is mostly free and overshoot is mostly not: interpolating a trajectory
costs almost nothing, while holding overshoot down under a tight deadline is where
the control effort goes. The coupling result is the one that tends to land. People
quantize a model for a latency win, see the accuracy drop as a small number on a
benchmark, and miss that the same drop is centimeters of sensing error in a room
with a child in it. Measuring the envelope before and after turns that abstract
accuracy loss into the distance it really is.

## Read

Keep the control operational, not a course. Smooth motion here is trajectory
interpolation, the minimum-jerk profiles of Flash and Hogan (1985); holding a
target against disturbance is PID and, where contact matters, impedance control.
The deeper point is not the controller. It is the budget the controller lives
inside, and the chain that connects a model's precision to a body's safety.

::: {.callout-teaching}

- **Hook**: the same gesture rendered jerky and then min-jerk; let students feel
  the difference before measuring it. The felt difference earns the math.
- **Watch**: how much control theory for an engineer audience? Keep it
  operational. The chapter's job is the coupling between model and motion, not a
  derivation of PID.
- **Open question**: this is the clearest place to make the MCU and MPU split
  concrete, control on one, intent on the other. Introduce the shared-memory
  handoff here, or assume the harness from the foundations lab?

:::
